news.body:
开普勒互动首度公开新作《坦克狂途》实机演示。在一段全新实机演示片段中，Alpha Channel 与 Kepler Interactive 揭晓了备受期待的坦克动作游戏《坦克狂途》（TankRat）此前从未公开的全新细节 。
本次实机演示的核心是“铁袭”（Ironstrike）任务——这是《坦克狂途》中的一个全新关卡，在其前作《TankHead》中从未出现过 。随着主角惠特克（Whittaker）踏上寻找其现已数字化的自我的原始副本——即他的“零号人格”（Persona Zero）的旅程，玩家得以从全新视角一窥这个世界的背景设定 。一路上，仅凭神秘向导西里尔（Cyril）提供的一条线索，惠特克深入探索了邻近城市“铁袭”的废墟，并逐渐揭开这座昔日辉煌之城崩塌的真相 。
实机演示还展示了《坦克狂途》让玩家在事件遏制区（ECA）大肆破坏、将其他坦克拆得七零八落的全新方式之一——“远程操控仪”（Remote Viewer） 。这一全新机制允许玩家暂时夺取敌方单位的控制权，并用他们自己的武器反戈一击，将他们的盟友撕成碎片 。
“铁袭”任务的尾声将迎来与头目“电缆蠕虫”（Cableworm）的决战 。这是一个由“铁袭”周围地形融合而成的恐怖机甲混合体，它能从地面撕扯下金属并赋予其生命 。当它用九叉激光倾泻恐怖火力时，如果你想要活着逃出生天，你的坦克必须足够敏捷以闪避攻击，或者足够坚固以承受爆炸冲击 。在整场战斗中，体型较小的“坦克狂途”单位——抓取者（Grabbers），还会试图用辐射让你的坦克和核心指针（Needle）过载 。
在惠特克的旅途中，他还将遇到《坦克狂途》的全新 NPC 之一——名为薇洛（Willow）的令人不寒而栗的生物 。作为西里尔的老朋友，以及首批通过“远程投影”（Teleprojection）上传意识的“高点”（Highpoint）居民之一，薇洛被独自遗留在 ECA 的时间太长了 。她的理智之弦已紧绷到了极限，并向惠特克透露了许多关于他未来的、或许令他难以接受的真相 。
梦行者们将于 1 月 15 日在 PlayStation 5 和 PC（Steam）平台正式出击 。立即添加至愿望单吧 。

members.title: EVE Online Dev Open-Sources Its Physically Based SSAO Technology
Eve Online maker Fenris Creations is adding a rendering technique to its open-source Carbon engine that promises more accurate shading and greater depth

news.body:
EVE Online Dev Open-Sources Its Physically Based SSAO Technology
CORTAO is now available for you to explore, integrate, and build upon.
Fenris Creations, the studio best known for EVE Online, has introduced CORTAO (Circular Occluder Ray-Traced Ambient Occlusion), which makes game worlds look more realistic with better shading and a stronger sense of depth, without putting too much strain on performance. The studio has also made the technology open-source through its Carbon engine framework.
Senior Rendering Engineer Daniel Isheden originally developed CORTAO as an independent project, which later became a full production tool with the studio's support. The team at Fenris Creations has used the technology in EVE Frontier, an upcoming space survival MMO, giving it a chance to perform across vastly different scales: massive open spaces, large-scale battles, megastructures, and enclosed interiors.
CORTAO takes a different approach to screen-space ambient occlusion: it uses information from what's currently visible on screen to represent nearby surfaces as circular occluders, helping calculate how they block ambient light. Testing reportedly shows this approach improves visual accuracy while keeping rendering costs low, with particularly strong results in visually complex scenes.
"Ambient occlusion adds the subtle darkening that occurs where nearby surfaces block light from the environment. It helps objects feel grounded in their surroundings and makes the shape and detail of complex scenes easier to read. CORTAO improves the accuracy and stability of this effect, reducing the dark halos and distracting shifts in shading that can appear around objects as the camera moves.
CORTAO calculates this shading in real time without requiring baked scene data, making it well suited to environments that players continually build and reshape. From the contact between small objects to the overlapping structures of a vast installation, the technique helps preserve a consistent sense of depth as the scene changes."
Here's how CORTAO compares to the existing state of the art, called Ground Truth Ambient Occlusion, according to its developer:
- CORTAO provides a never-before-seen level of physical accuracy rivaling that of brute-force hardware ray tracing, while only relying on screen-space information;
- CORTAO handles depth discontinuities in complex scenes in a more conservative way, avoiding the view-dependent occlusion of GTAO and producing less obvious artifacts when screen space information is limited;
- CORTAO, at the same time, has greatly improved convergence, producing much higher-quality results at lower sample counts even for scenes where GTAO works well, which is especially important for low-end hardware.
Daniel Isheden and Fenris Creations have put together a well-prepared release, giving graphics programmers the freedom to experiment with CORTAO, adapt it to their own projects, and contribute improvements. No AI was involved in the development of CORTAO.
You can find the original CORTAO's source code and documentation here, and the Carbon-optimized version here. For a closer look at how the technique works, including visual comparisons and performance benchmarks, you can visit this page.

members.title: Witcher 3 devs use AI to help Polish voice actor reprise role of Geralt after stroke
CD Projekt Red used AI to alter the voice of Geralt's original Polish actor in Witcher 3: Songs of the Past

news.body:
Witcher 3 devs use AI to help Polish voice actor reprise role of Geralt after stroke
After a stroke left him unable to do the voice of the Witcher series' main character anymore, Jacek Rozenek consented to using AI for Witcher 3's next expansion.
Original Polish voice actor for The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt protagonist Geralt of Rivia Jacek Rozenek has consented to a special exception for CD Projekt Red to use AI to aid his voice acting in the announced expansion to the 11-year-old game, specifically for the purpose of maintaining continuity in his performance after his voice was changed following a stroke.
As reported by Game File, the discussion began when CDPR brought Rozenek in to discuss returning for the upcoming expansion, Songs of the Past. As an unprecedented late expansion to the 2015 game, the new lines would be in close proximity to thousands of lines Rozenek had recorded as the Polish voice of Geralt well over a decade ago, but due tohis stroke, Rozenek sounds different. Thus, the decision was made to use AI to bridge the gap.
Rozenek had returned to acting in the years after his stroke, but the job drained him physically, and he sounded gruffer and lower than he had years prior. In a brand new project, maybe that wouldn't make a big difference, but it would have been immediately noticeable when positioned next to recordings from a decade prior.
CD Projekt Red made the decision to call on Respeecher, a professional AI voice generator that the studio has used before to use the voice of a late actor in Cyberpunk 2077's Phantom Liberty expansion. Rozenek agreed, allowing the studio to take his recordings for Songs of the Past—which he was still being hired and paid for—and use AI to make it sound more like it used to. The AI tools involved were trained on Rozenek's previous recordings over the prior Witcher games.
"I do think this is one of those ways where you can use AI ethically, with consent and also to do something good," says localization producer Mikołaj Szwed. Szwed stresses this is not a common occurrence and this exception was only being made due to Rozenek's health.
It is unknown if Rozenek will reprise the role of Geralt in the Polish version of The Witcher 4, but a different, deeper voice for Geralt might make more sense in a sequel rather than an expansion to an older game.

news.title: Rules, states, and win conditions in video games: a guide
news.summary_raw: Learn how rules, game states, and win and lose conditions work in video games, with simple examples and a five-step method to define yours before you build.

members.title: Rules, states, and win conditions in video games: a guide

news.body:
Rules, states, and win conditions in video games: a guide
Unity Team - Unity Technologies
Learn how rules, game states, and win and lose conditions work in video games, with simple examples and a five-step method to define yours before you build.
Nearly every video game makes three promises to the player. It tells them what they can do, it remembers what has happened so far, and it decides when the game is over. Those promises have names: rules, states, and win and lose conditions.
You don’t need to write code to design them. You do need to decide on them. A game with great art and a vague answer to “How do I win?” will leave players confused. This guide explains each idea in plain language, shows how they fit together, and ends with a short method for defining them for your own game.
What are rules in a video game?
Rules define what players can and can’t do in a game, and what happens as a result of doing those things. Rules create structure and limits, which keeps the game consistent and fair. If your core game loop is the action players repeat, rules decide what that action can do and change.
A useful way to sort rules is by how each rule works. Setup rules cover what happens once, at the start. Progression rules cover what happens during play. Resolution rules cover what ends the game and how you decide the outcome. Some rules are automatic, such as a bonus timer that counts down every second. Others define the choices players can make and what those choices change, such as deciding whether to use a key on a locked shortcut, which opens a faster route but leaves one fewer key for the exit.
A simple two-player grid game shows all three. For example:
- Setup: Draw a grid and pick who goes first.
- Progression: On your turn, mark an empty square, then pass play to your opponent.
- Resolution: Three marks in a row wins, and a full board with no winner is a draw.
Here are a few more made-up examples demonstrating this idea in a video game context:
Good rules make the goal harder to reach
Most designers aim to make products as simple to use as possible. Games work the other way: once you’ve set a goal for the player, your job is to put obstacles in their way. If the goal takes no effort, winning has no thrill. If it’s too hard, the player never gets to win, which is frustrating.
Clarity matters just as much. When players spend time figuring out what they’re allowed to do, the confusion pulls them out of the game. Write rules so a new player can quickly determine what is and isn’t possible in your video game.
Unwritten rules still count
Players also bring assumptions based on what they’ve played previously. A common example in shooter-style games is spawn camping: waiting beside the spot where defeated players reappear and defeating them before they can react. Some players call that smart strategy. Others call it cheap. The rules allow it, so whether it’s fair depends on unwritten expectations.
The lesson is to define as many rules as you can, so players don’t argue about them or exploit gaps you didn’t see. Playtesting your video game is one of the best ways to find those gaps.
What is a game state?
A game state is the game’s current situation: where things are, what the score is, how much health is left, and which part of the game you’re in. Rules are what change the state.
Most games depend heavily on state. Character animations change depending on whether the player is walking, jumping, or standing. Enemy behavior can change depending on whether the enemy is chasing the player or fleeing from them. Players can change the game state at will by pausing, opening a menu, or loading a save file.
Most games share a few flow states
Think of the overall flow of your game as a small set of modes, with exactly one active at a time. A common set looks like this:
The player resumes
The player resumes
Beginner tutorials also treat these modes as a small set of named phases, with each phase handling its own screen. Gameplay updates belong only in the playing state, so nothing moves while a menu is open.
Many games add more states, such as a win screen, a level-complete screen, or a cutscene (a short clip breaking up gameplay and advancing a game’s progression or narrative). Add one whenever the game needs to behave differently for a while.
If you’re building without code, you’ll still make these decisions. What happens when the player pauses? What do they see when they lose? How fast can they try again? Drawing the states as boxes and arrows on paper is enough to answer these questions before you start building a user interface for your video game.
Win and lose conditions explained
Win and lose conditions are the rules that define how a player wins or loses the game, or at least a section or level. They are the resolution rules from earlier, and they give every other rule its purpose. We’ve included several examples of win and lose conditions below:
Securing a resource advantage
Securing a resource advantage
What makes a good game goal?
Players should never have to ask whether they’ve won. If they do, the goal is probably too vague. A good goal is also attractive: the act of reaching it should sound enjoyable. And it should be exact, even if the ways of reaching it are flexible. If you start by naming the feeling you want players to have, check that your goal serves it.
Goals can work on three time scales:
- Short-term goals are bite-sized and give quick feedback.
- Mid-term goals take longer but fit within a session or a few sessions.
- Long-term goals give the whole game a direction.
Objectives are the stepping stones between them. Some are required, some are optional, and some are timed. Time pressure adds tension, so use it carefully unless it’s central to your core loop.
Four questions to ask about every game ending
For each game, and each level, ask:
- How can the player win?
- How can the player lose?
- Can the game end in a draw, or get stuck so that neither is possible?
- What happens right after: what does the player see, and what can they do next?
The third question catches endings you didn’t plan for. In the grid example, you write the draw into the rules on purpose. An ending you didn’t plan for, like a level players can no longer finish, can leave players stuck with no way forward.
How to keep players invested in your game
First, players disengage once they believe they can’t win. A catch-up feature, such as a swing in luck or a bonus for those who are behind, gives players something to hope for.
Second, a game should push toward its own ending. Length is a common problem in first designs, and a game should end before players want to stop. In a video game, that might mean difficulty ramps up, a timer runs, or each level has a clear exit.
Putting it together
Imagine a one-screen game where you collect three keys and reach an exit while dodging moving hazards.
- Rules: You start with three lives. Touching a hazard costs a life. Collecting all three keys opens the exit.
- States: title screen, playing, paused, win, game over
- Win condition: Reach the open exit.
- Lose condition: Lose all three lives.
- After the ending: The win screen shows your time. The game over screen offers “Try again,” which returns to playing.
That’s a complete game structure in a few lines, and it’s the same structure a much larger game builds on.
How to define your game’s rules, states, and win conditions in five steps
Work through these five steps in order to define your game’s rules, states, and win conditions:
- Write the goal in one sentence. What is the player trying to do?
- List your rules in three groups: setup, progression, and resolution.
- Name your states and draw the arrows between them. Check that the player can always get from one to another.
- Write every ending: each way to win, each way to lose, and what happens next.
- Playtest and watch for the question “Did I win?” If a tester asks it, your goal or ending needs work.
If you’re working from our one-page game design plan, steps one through four map directly to its goal, win, and lose section.
A rules, states, and endings checklist
Consider checking your game against this list:
- I can state the goal in one sentence.
- My rules are sorted into setup, progression, and resolution.
- I’ve named each state and know how players move between them.
- I know every way to win and every way to lose.
- Players can tell when they have won or lost without a message telling them.
- My win and lose signals don’t rely on color or sound alone.
- Losing doesn’t leave players stuck: they know what to do next.
- I’ve watched at least three people play and noted where they were unsure what the rules allowed.
Decide the structure, then build on it
Rules tell players what they can do. States keep track of where the game is. Win and lose conditions tell players when it’s over. Define all three before you build, so the rest of your design – levels, enemies, and interface – sits on a solid foundation.
Ready to turn your plan into a video game? You don’t need to be a developer. Try Unity Spark, Unity’s browser-based, AI game creation platform that allows you to describe your game, refine it in a real web editor, and publish it for others to play.

members.title: Epic is Taking Apple's 27% Web Fee to the Supreme Court

news.body:
Epic is Taking Apple's 27% Web Fee to the Supreme Court
Epic argues that Apple deliberately combined its commission with payment-processing costs and restrictive link designs to make alternative purchasing systems economically unviable.eee
According to a new GamesBeat report, Epic Games has filed a brief with the U.S. Supreme Court asking it to preserve a contempt ruling against Apple over restrictions imposed on external purchases.
The dispute centers on the 27% commission Apple introduced for purchases completed on the web within seven days of a user following a link from an iOS app. Epic CEO Tim Sweeney has described the charge as a “junk fee,” while the company’s legal filing argues that Apple deliberately made alternative payment systems economically unviable for developers.
Apple normally collects as much as 30% through its in-app purchasing system. According to Epic, developers using a web payment provider would still owe Apple 27% while separately paying more than 3% in payment-processing costs. The combined expense could consequently exceed Apple’s standard commission.
“As a result, developers actually would lose money by directing consumers to external payment systems,” Epic’s filing states. It also cites an Apple executive who acknowledged that linked-out transactions would be more expensive for developers than purchases processed through Apple at 30%.
Epic claims that Apple “reverse engineered” the rate to discourage developers from offering alternative payment options. The commission was accompanied by requirements governing the design and placement of external links, restrictions on dynamic URLs, approved language, and a full-page warning shown before users could leave an app.
The legal battle began after Epic bypassed Apple’s payment system inside Fortnite in 2020. Apple removed the game from the App Store, prompting Epic to sue. Although Epic lost most of its antitrust claims, courts determined that Apple could not prevent developers from informing customers about other purchasing methods.
Fortnite
Apple responded by allowing certain external links while introducing the 27% commission and additional design restrictions. In April 2025, District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers found Apple in willful violation of the earlier injunction and prohibited it from collecting commissions on off-app purchases. The decision gave U.S. developers considerably more freedom to promote and operate their own web stores.
The ruling subsequently helped clear the way for Fortnite to return to the U.S. App Store after an absence of nearly five years.
An appeals court upheld the contempt finding but ruled that banning every possible external-purchase fee was too broad. Apple may eventually be permitted to collect a limited amount covering costs genuinely necessary to support external links, but it cannot currently charge a commission until the district court approves an appropriate fee

Apple argues that it should not have been held in contempt because the original injunction never expressly prohibited commissions. Epic counters that this interpretation would let companies circumvent court orders by replacing prohibited practices with new restrictions that produce the same result.
The Supreme Court is therefore considering the legal standard for contempt rather than directly deciding whether 27% is a reasonable fee. Oral arguments are scheduled for January 11, 2027.

news.title: How to protect your IP against the army of AI clones
news.summary_raw: Generative AI usage in video game development has increased significantly in recent months. Steam Next Fest featured over 8,000 demos in October 2026, many of which were created partly or entirely using generative AI tools.

members.title: How to protect your IP against the army of AI clones
"It's a wild situation" – An investor and publisher perspective on the rise of AI copycats, the discoverability crisis, and more

news.body:
How to protect your IP against the army of AI clones
Pryor Cashman's lawyers provide some practical tips for ensuring you're protected under US law if your game is copied by generative AI
Generative AI usage in video game development has increased significantly in recent months. Steam Next Fest featured over 8,000 demos in October 2026, many of which were created partly or entirely using generative AI tools.
Unfortunately, but unsurprisingly, AI is facilitating a new wave of rapidly assembled, unauthorised clones, mods, and ports of existing games. And developers are starting to report cancelling public demos for fear of being cloned before they can even get their games to market.
The new paradigm might turn conventional logic on its head. For decades, games have been previewed via journalistic features, trailers, and demos. More recently, early access has given developers an opportunity to test features and build their audiences by letting them try the game as the developer iterates, while some in the industry have encouraged developers to share early prototypes on social media to gauge audience reaction before committing to production. This may prove to be a risky proposition in the generative AI era.
Given the unprecedented ability of this new technology to misappropriate games that have taken years and often millions of dollars to create, what can developers do to protect their games under US law?
#1 Ensure confidentiality
Developers should engage in a risk assessment when sharing their in-progress work. The genre and type of game might help to determine how susceptible it is to cloning – games reliant on unique mechanics might be more at risk than heavily story-based games, or those with a strong existing brand or IP.
It is best practice from a legal perspective to require NDAs when sharing footage, demos, and codes
Some developers will elect to engage in private playtesting in lieu of early access or public demos. With that said, it is best practice from a legal perspective to require NDAs when sharing footage, demos, and codes, prohibiting any sharing of confidential information, recording, or video capture of gameplay – as well as any inputting of game-related media and information into any LLM, chatbot, or similar generative AI technology. This can happen in concert with practical measures such as watermarking – which can also assist later with proving infringement at the enforcement stage (see #6) – along with password protection, and revocable/limited-time access.
Moreover, to the extent that parties are being asked to provide feedback, it would be best practice to ensure that the paperwork confirms that any suggestions or contributions to the game are made on a work-for-hire basis and, in the alternative, are assigned exclusively to the developer. This includes employees, independent contractors, composers, voice actors, and outside studios, who should also obtain corresponding agreements from their personnel so all relevant rights flow back to the ultimate rightsholder.
Certain subsets of the video game industry are, by their nature, collaborative and informal, and that orientation to community engagement can produce incredible results. But developers must strike a balance between frictionless sharing and measures to protect their valuable IP. Standardised, developer-friendly agreements and clear contributor processes can help preserve that collaborative culture without leaving ownership gaps that complicate future licensing, publishing, financing, or enforcement.
#2 Understand your contractors' and collaborators' use of AI
As the rightsholder, it is important to understand how other people touching the IP are using generative AI technologies. Different studios have different approaches around AI – we have clients that are "zero AI" and others that are embracing the technologies.
The key for each company is to develop a policy and ensure that its employees, vendors, and contractors comply with that use. You don't want to open the door to infringement, or lose trade-secret protections over your code, because a contractor has made confidential information and proprietary systems available to third parties using AI without your knowledge or approval.
#3 Register copyrights
Prior to any publicity or release of the game, developers or the ultimate rightsholders should file applications with the US Copyright Office to register their copyrights in and to the game's script and narrative materials, character designs and biographies, key art, concept art, original music and sound recordings, trailer footage, and other sufficiently developed, copyrightable assets. In the US, a copyright registration (not merely a pending application) is generally required before a rightsholder can bring a federal infringement action involving a US work.
As explained below (#6), having a copyright registration already in place is critical to your ability to move swiftly to enforce your rights in a US court. Timely copyright registration can also unlock significant financial remedies: in the US, this can include statutory damage awards of up to $150,000 for willful infringement (without requiring proof of actual, financial damages), as well as attorneys' fees. Again, the timing of registration is important, as these remedies are often unavailable if, for example, a developer only seeks registration after the infringement occurs.
#4 Register trademarks
Trademark registration provides an additional, distinct layer of protection. Developers should consider applying to register the game's name as a trademark with the US Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) on an intent-to-use basis several months before the game's planned public release. Other assets, such as a game’s characters, may also be registered in certain cases if used as part of the game's branding.
A federal trademark registration generally strengthens enforcement options
The trademark application process with the USPTO is currently taking around 10 months from start to finish and, instead of waiting to file a registration application until the game is released, rightsholders can submit the application early and go through the examination process and other parts of the application process to receive a Notice of Allowance and then submit a Statement of Use showing use of the trademark in commerce once the game is publicly released.
Although common-law trademark rights may develop as soon as the game is released, a federal trademark registration generally strengthens enforcement options, especially when submitting trademark infringement notices to third-party distribution platforms.
#5 Build a brand, secure socials
One of the strongest protections against AI cloning in the longer term is to build a brand. To that end, rightsholders should consider securing relevant domain names and social media handles to head off cybersquatting that could divert web traffic away from official publishing platforms.
Rightsholders should prioritise the principal domain-name variations and social handles associated with the game, its studio, and any major franchise or character brands. A registered trademark can strengthen enforcement options against bad actors, including under ICANN's Uniform Domain-Name Dispute-Resolution Policy (UDRP) and most third-party distribution platforms' impersonation and trademark notice-and-takedown regimes.
#6 Enforce your rights
Once you have obtained the protections outlined above, you will be in a stronger position to enforce your rights against infringing third parties, often by leveraging multiple types of IP protections. Setting up ongoing monitoring systems is key, and different resources are available for detecting unauthorised use of your game, including professional service providers who are experienced in finding online infringement.
When unauthorised copies of a game are discovered, the response may include sending a cease-and-desist letter or takedown notice, or filing a civil lawsuit (or some combination). Filing a lawsuit and getting a preliminary injunction from a court is a powerful tool to prevent the release and distribution of unauthorised clones, but moving swiftly is essential. When seeking a preliminary injunction in US courts, a developer must show that it faces "irreparable harm" if the infringement is not immediately halted, and any prior delay in the developer's exercise of its rights may undermine that claim in the eyes of the court.
It is important to have a US copyright registration in place before any infringement starts
Of course, it is already in developers' business interest to move quickly to stamp out unauthorised clones, as each day those clones are available in the marketplace they can cause consumer confusion and siphon sales. For these reasons and those explained in #3, it is important to have a US copyright registration in place before any infringement starts in the first place.
Digital channels and generative AI tools are eroding many traditional protections for game developers – including "time to market." Accordingly, a good IP attorney who knows the games industry can be an important tool in your arsenal. Your attorney can ensure that your agreements are comprehensively drafted, copyright and trademark registration applications are properly completed and filed in a timely manner, and marketplaces, app stores, and social platforms are monitored, as well as putting in place a rapid-response protocol to infringement that includes platform complaints, cease-and-desist letters, and litigation.
The practical objective is to have chain-of-title documentation, registrations, and enforcement procedures ready before the first public reveal, and not to begin building that infrastructure after infringement has already spread.
Simon Pulman and Josh Weigensberg are partners, and Joshua Greenberg is counsel, in Pryor Cashman's Interactive+Gaming practice group.

members.title: Steam's submission and approval backlog is forcing indie devs to delay game launches

news.body:
Steam's submission and approval backlog is forcing indie devs to delay game launches
Valve has been working over "the last several weeks to scale [its] process to match demand"
Several indie developers have had to postpone their game launches due to delays in Steam's game submission and approval process.
Developer Rami Ismail told Eurogamer that the latest build of Australia Did It: End-of-the-World Railway Defense Business, co-developed with Aesthetican Labs, has been in Steam's approval queue since October 20, 2026.
"[It] failed over a minor controller input on November 5 (which we resolved the same day), and we've been waiting again since with no meaningful response from Valve despite follow-ups."
"I'm used to hold-and-wait patterns on console, but Steam has historically been much more snappy – 10 to 14 days pre-launch was usually enough to fail twice and ship on time," added Ismail.
Eurogamer also cited other indie developers experiencing delays, including TwoMenGames, Monoii Studio, and Studio Daimon.
Last week, Valve acknowledged a "significant increase in submissions for store page and build review in recent months" and stated it has been working over "the last several weeks to scale our process to match it."
"We aim to test every game build in a timely manner, typically within three to five business days," it said. "However, we're running a little behind right now, and it's taking up to 12 business days. Much of that delay is due to having to re-review games."
Last month, concerns were raised about an increase in 'AI slop' on Steam, specifically that generative AI is being used to clone games, especially indie titles.
Valve did not attribute the slowdown to the influx of generative AI-developed games, but Ismail expressed concern that Valve's lack of acknowledgement could harm developers over time.
"I am concerned that Valve trying to avoid taking a political position on AI is forcing them into choices that will inevitably be worse for developers," he said.
"If sloppers can submit several game clones a day through automated systems, the only way for Valve to stem the tide of games damaging genuine developers' work is to put constraints on game distribution, increase fees, or make the process more complicated."
"In the 'open market' Valve seems to so adore, they're going to be the ones carrying the costs for moderation, so I don't think they'll like the open market on this – but there's no outcome of this that allows Valve neutrality on AI and not do things that will ultimately make life worse for developers."
Earlier this year, Valve amended its AI disclosure policy on Steam, requiring developers to disclose use of the technology only in specific cases, such as content generation.
The company has also allowed "the vast majority of games" using AI on its platform since 2024.

news.body:
《魔域》年终重大活动「世界树：天痕之上」将于2026年12月18日全面上线。本次更新除了神火与副本，在装备系统上也迎来了升级，全新圣装精炼系统与副本轮换机制同步登场。本文围绕活动上线节点、千万魔石预约福利以及圣装系统的具体调整进行梳理。

members.title: MapleStory franchise Q3 revenue rises 72%, drives overall growth for Nexon

news.body:
MapleStory franchise Q3 revenue rises 72%, drives overall growth for Nexon
FC, Dungeon & Fighter, and MapleStory franchises collectively delivered $678.4 million in revenue
Nexon reported increases across the board during its third quarter, which were all above the company's outlook for the period.
Its results were driven by its three largest franchises – MapleStory, Dungeon & Fighter, and FC – which collectively delivered ¥108.5 billion ($678.4 million) in revenue, up 24% year-on-year.
The numbers
- Revenue: ¥138.4 billion ($865.4 million), up 17% year-on-year
- Operating income: ¥41.8 billion ($261.3 million), up 11% year-on-year
- Net income: ¥38.1 billion ($238.2 million), flat year-on-year
The highlights
Nexon's third quarter operating income benefited from higher royalties from FC Online and MapleStory: Idle RPG, which were "more than offset by lower marketing, HR, and cloud costs."
MapleStory franchise revenue grew 72% year-over-year, setting a new quarterly record and driving most of Nexon's revenue.
FC achieved double-digit growth, while Dungeon & Fighter revenue declined 33% due to "weaker-than-expected results from the September National Day updates in China."
Embark Studios' Arc Raiders has sold over 17 million copies to date. Last month, the third-person shooter launched its Frozen Trail update, which was "successful in reengaging lapsed players and driving incremental unit sales."
Nexon also announced Project Overkill, a new online RPG set in the Dungeon & Fighter universe. Neople is developing the title, and Tencent will publish it.
As part of Nexon's ongoing transformation initiative introduced earlier this year, six projects were discontinued in recent months, with "budgets and creative teams redeployed to games with greater commercial viability."
Nexon also provided an update on AI integration, which is "accelerating across development, localisation, and code review to enable developers to spend more time taking creative risks and validating new ideas."
"The aim is to create more ambitious, higher-quality games with the teams already in place, not to make the same games at lower cost," the company clarified. "Nexon's games are made by people, and that is not changing."
"Our IP expansion strategy is delivering clear results," said Nexon president and CEO Junghun Lee.
"Diversified revenue from brand extensions in established franchises like MapleStory, along with FC's return to growth, and new games like Arc Raiders, strengthens our core business and reduces dependence on any single franchise or market."
"Additionally, the third quarter reflects the impact of our transformation initiative in guiding decisions on where we invest talented people and capital to build games with strong commercial potential."

news.body:
A second 2026 State of the Game Industry survey? It can happen! ft. Beth Elderkin & Imran Khan
On this week's BONUS episode of the GameDeveloper.com Podcast, we're diving into a second GDC Festival of Gaming State of the Industry report with all-new data on the world of game development
November 12, 2026
It's time again for the annual GDC Festival of Gaming State of the Industry report. Except, unusually, it's the second time this year for the release of this report.
Why two "annual" reports in one year? It's because going forward, GDC Festival of Gaming organizers plan to release the report toward the end of the year instead of at the beginning. That meant either waiting 18 months for another report, or doubling up for two in one year.
Regardless, report means another round of excellent data to inform the game development community. Today we're diving into the results with GDC content marketing manager Beth Elderkin and GameDeveloper.com contributing editor Imran Khan to discuss topics like layoffs, excess overtime, and the use of generative AI.
About the Game Developer Podcast
The Game Developer podcast is a bi-weekly podcast chronicling the triumphs, catastrophes, and everything in-between of game development, sharing lessons and strategies fellow developers can use to hone their craft. The Game Developer Podcast is hosted by Bryant Francis, edited by Pierre Landriau, and features music by Mike Meehan.
Follow Game Developer on Bluesky or on LinkedIn.
Game Developer, and Omdia and GDC Festival of Gaming are sibling organizations under Informa Festivals.

features.title: Secrets of the Blast Mask (and Retro Gaming Magic)
features.summary_raw: No, you won’t. Not if you know the trick. The Blast Mask’s description hides a huge secret. Much of “retro game magic” comes from designs that follow this pattern. Bombs are an important exploration tool in Majora’s Mask. You use them to blow open secret areas. It’s annoying when you run out of bombs, which […]
features.rss_content: No, you won’t. Not if you know the trick. The Blast Mask’s description hides a huge secret. Much of “retro game magic” comes from designs that follow this pattern. Bombs are an important exploration tool in Majora’s Mask. You use them to blow open secret areas. It’s annoying when you run out of bombs, which is one reason Breath of the Wild just gave you an infinite source from your magical smartphone. Majora’s Mask’s solution: Gve the player a reusable bomb, as long as they strap it to their face. It’s a useful item with an interesting tradeoff, but the coolest moment is when you figure out the trick. The Trick: If you’re raising your Shield whien you detonate the Blast Mask, you don’t take damage from the explosion. This makes no thematic sense. The shield is in front of your face. The Mask is alreaady ON your face. It’s a quirk of the game’s coding. It’s also a fantastic moment that makes players feel awesome, and makes them wonder what else there is to discover. The “hand-holding” discussion in modern games misses the point. If players universaly liked feeling lost, there wouldn’t have been such a big market for Strategy Guides. I read so many cover to cover. Here’s why the Blast Mask works better: You don’t need to know this trick to play the game. It’s “Optional Complexity”. It’s a glitch, but I’d never fix it. It rewards players for experimenting, exploring, and makes them want to share the knowledge with others. Heck, I’m doing that now. Confusing, counter-intuitive game behavior liek this is a HUGE problem if you HAVE to know it to play the game. “How could I have guessed that?!?” we rightly shout. Shielding the Blast Mask is the opposite. It’s why Minecraft is so fun to get into. You don’t need to know that being in a boat negates fall damage. You don’t need to know you can make an infinite water source from two water blocks placed in opposing diagonal corners of a 2×2 square. But, when you learn that, it makes an immediate and exciting difference to how you play. So try the pattern: Design useful secrets that are a bit counter-intuitive, the kind most people won’t stumble across. As long as you don’t NEED to know them to have fun playing the game, you’ll spark joy for people who figure it out. It’s pretty cool. If you like my breakdowns, you should check out my design bootcamp: Mastering Game Systems . Now, back to the Moon.

members.title: 沉迷《深空当铺》50小时后，我专访了游戏主创Bei Ning Pan

features.body:
实不相瞒，上周我已经在最近正式发售的《深空当铺：可能是偷的》里沉迷了近50小时了，而且游戏时长还在增长中。
其实早在游戏Demo上线之际，我就已经开始了自己的当铺老板之旅。在这个赛博朋克题材的经营模拟游戏里头，玩家需要经营一间当铺：没有倒计时的紧迫感，也没有传统意义上的最终Boss——你可以在柜台前无尽地发愣、理货、算账，唯一不断上涨的，是光头的黑心房东漫天要价的店铺房租。
毫无疑问，它的创作灵感来自《十三号空间站》和《请出示证件》，但游戏又充满自己的特色：白天在柜台后接待形形色色的顾客，分辨哪些人是普通客人，哪些客人根本不是人类，哪些人其实是罪犯要销赃，还有哪些人是通缉犯……而夜里则可以出门，在宇宙中拾荒碰运气，或是去升级装备，扩大店铺经营范围，把自己的小店做大做强。
前段时间，主创Bei Ning Pan通过邮件接受了我的专访，聊了聊Demo的内容、正式发售之后的定价考量、柜台时间静止的设计初衷，以及玩法平衡的故事等等。
G=Gamecores
B=Bei Ning Pan
一、从Demo到1.0：一间宇宙中的当铺是怎么开起来的？
先从最现实的地方说起吧！Demo上线之后，不少人（包括我）已经在柜台后面耗掉了大把时间，那正式版究竟多给了什么，又凭什么定这个价呢？
G：在试玩Demo时我注意到，目前只开放了少数几个职业和玩法风格，游戏的其他一些内容也还没有完全开放。能否谈谈正式版在Demo之外还会包含哪些内容，以及你们对定价是怎么考虑的？
B：既然游戏已经发售，我就可以聊聊我们是怎么决定定价的了。对我们来说非常重要的一点是，价格要和游戏的内容量相匹配，而且要照顾到每个地区的玩家。发行方必须考虑各地区的购买力，为游戏单独设定本地价格，他们还咨询了社区玩家对定价的预期。最终我认为他们做得非常出色。很多评测都提到，相对于这样的内容量，这个价格非常公道，我们对此相当开心。在官方公布价格之前，每当玩家问起定价，我都会开玩笑说，这游戏大概值“三个巨无霸”汉堡——因为巨无霸的价格也是按地区购买力调整的。这个梗后来在社区里小范围传开了。
G：从Demo到完整版的这些职业当中，有没有哪一条路线是你格外偏爱的？哪一个是你们最先确定下来的？
B：我们开发的每一个新职业，通常都比前一个需要更多工作量。最初，职业不过是一组初始物品，仅此而已。随着开发推进，每个新职业都变得更复杂、更花时间。我觉得水培农夫、化学家和枪械匠我们做得非常好。它们是最新的几个，也是到目前为止投入最多的。
简单来说，这是一款完全没有即时反应事件（QTE），也完全没有Boss的游戏。如果让我形容游玩时的感受，第一个跑到我头脑中的词汇是“从容”。但没有倒计时，并不代表着游戏内容不会令人紧张。
G：游戏没有最终Boss——只有一个不断上涨的房租。我很想知道是什么让你们做出了这样的设计。我现在已经把不断上涨的房租当成最终Boss 了，这和你对它的理解一致吗？
B：在 Demo 阶段，我们希望提供一个开放式的体验，因为游戏是沙盒和模拟类。但我们也无法把所有内容都塞进Demo。由于买下店铺就代表通关一次，我们认为它不应该被包含在内。考虑到Demo本身已经相当慷慨，这一点尤其成立。有些玩家在Demo里已经玩了一百多个小时。
比起一笔按月上涨的房租，我更想聊的是另一件事：站在柜台后面的时候，整个世界的时间是停住的。
G：游戏里我最喜欢的一点是，站在柜台后面时，时间是静止的。很多同类经营游戏会用倒计时来制造紧迫感，所以这个设计显得格外慷慨，也让游戏玩起来很享受。这样做主要是为了让玩家能从容地整理账本吗？我一直觉得，在没人催你的时候，这种复盘总结会显得温柔很多。这里头也有这层考虑吗？既然没有倒计时，你们靠什么来维持张力？
B：我认为去掉即时反应事件（QTE）会让游戏更好玩，也能让更多类型的玩家享受它。《深空当铺》大概有一层赛博朋克的皮，但玩起来非常像一款舒适向（cozy）游戏。游戏里没有紧急的实时目标，但有关键目标，比如交房租，这些是按游戏内天数来计算的。我们就是这样维持张力的。
不过时间只在柜台后面停住。一旦你决定在打烊后关店出门，就会付出额外的代价了！
G：晚上出门拾荒，就意味着白天本可能上门的顾客不会出现了。这种离开的隐性代价是你们希望玩家感受到的吗？你们打算如何平衡“自由外出探索”和“留下来看店”这两种选择？
B：这个机制确实是为了让要不要出门这个决定更有深度，但我最初加它，主要是为了让玩家不会觉得必须每晚都出门——那样会变得很枯燥，好像不出门就白丢了多赚点钱的机会。有了这个机制，玩家可以安心决定不出门，而不会感到内疚。
总之呢，不论晚上关店出门也好，直接打烊守在店里也好，这间店最后还是要靠推门进来的形形色色的顾客们撑起门面。他们是些什么人，以及你在柜台后面听见了什么，决定了形形色色的分支剧情的走向。
G：顾客真的是一大惊喜——面孔那么多，而那些可疑的家伙确实让人过目不忘。在塑造他们的时候，有哪些细微的线索，能让玩家在一瞬间就感觉到：柜台前这个新来的客人，可能并不像表面看上去那样？
B：最初我们只有“通缉犯”顾客，他们的作用是为本来可能变得重复的玩法增加一点独特性。发行方的制作人Artyom Safarov提出，可以设计一类玩家能够开枪射杀的顾客，让游戏更有动感，于是我最终创作了Augs（义体人）。他们很合理地解释了，为什么一个普通店主会有一把霰弹枪，还被允许开枪“杀人”（尽管打的是义体人）。保持世界的沉浸感对我来说非常重要，而Augs这种无可救药、一见就必须射杀的存在，正好让我能实现射击机制。
G：每种玩法风格都有自己的赚钱方式。你希望怎样让它们都值得玩家投入时间，而不是所有人都涌向每分钟收益最高的那一种？如果某种风格被证明需要大量照料（比如养老鼠、养鱼或其他玩法）你会考虑简化操作步骤、调整数值，还是两者都做一点？
B：这一直是我们的一大难题。在公开Demo期间，我们收到大量玩家反馈，说水商相比其他玩法风格强得离谱，检查数值之后我们发现他们完全说得对。所以我在1.0版本里做了一组削弱，让水商和其他玩法更接近。结果这些改动受到了一些已经习惯了的玩家的强烈反对，他们觉得平衡调整过头了，所以我最后回调了其中一部分改动。我们会在发布任何新内容之前非常谨慎地确认平衡是否合适，以免之后又要做平衡调整。我们的目标是让每一种玩法风格都有趣、都有回报。
B：是的。我们有两位非常有才华的作曲家A.L.I.S.O.N和M. Harvey Bee，负责磁带的音乐。环境音效则由我们出色的声音设计师Sam Dalwood和Vasiliy Kashnikov制作。
最后，我想把话题交回给玩家——这间店能有今天，靠的是柜台外面那群人。
G：在玩家分享的所有内容里，有没有哪一条反馈最让你意外？
B：最让我意外的是玩家在 Demo 里花的时间。大家玩了那么久，我真的很震惊，哈哈。
从“三个巨无霸”的定价玩笑，到柜台后静止的时间，再到有所调整的数值变化，《深空当铺》确实是一款能让人充分体验赛博开店的游戏。游戏现已正式发售，如果你也想过一把赛博朋克当铺老板的瘾，不妨亲自到柜台后面站一站。
最后，感谢开发者抽出时间接受我的邮件专访，同时也祝各位玩家——也就是在这个茫茫宇宙中当铺的你，彩票期期中奖，拾荒回回丰收，顾客盈门，生意兴隆。

ai.title: datasette-leaflet 0.3
ai.summary_raw: Release: datasette-leaflet 0.3 OpenStreetMap have a very reasonable policy that hits to their hosted tile server should send a referrer header . Datasette table pages used the Referrer-Policy: no-referrer HTTP header, causing plugins that loaded tiles from OpenStreetMap to violate that policy. datasette-leaflet is the plugin that loads a bundled Leaflet so other Datasette plugins can depend on it. It now sets the referrer policy on the tile requests themselves to strict-origin-when-cross-origin , passing the host but not the full path to the page. Tags: leaflet , datasette , openstreetmap

members.title: openJiuwen发布RSI原生AgentOS，让Agent自由变身，持续迭代！

ai.body:
openJiuwen发布RSI原生AgentOS，让Agent自由变身，持续迭代！
想要什么功能，让Agent自己开发
允中 发自 凹非寺
量子位 | 公众号QbitAI
用WorkSwarm时，想加个新功能，能不能直接把需求告诉Agent，让它自己做出来，装上试试？
这个问题正好对应HyperAgent架构解读里谈到的扩展性。这是openJiuwen为HyperAgent提出的八项特征之一，即从「开发者友好」走向「RSI友好」。
扩展机制既要方便开发者接入新能力，也要让Agent能根据任务反馈动手改进自己的能力。改动做出来后，还得装进应用，在实际任务里试一试，才知道问题有没有解决，下一轮还要改哪里。
openJiuwen的RSI原生AgentOS，为这种递归自我改进（RSI）提供了运行环境。
它在界面、网关、服务端和Agent执行等环节提供不同类型的扩展点，覆盖运行全周期。新功能可以热插拔，接入时不用改应用原有代码。扩展包可以按版本管理，新版出了问题还能回退。
WorkSwarm用的就是这套扩展机制。它是基于openJiuwen RSI原生AgentOS构建的Agent应用。Agent可以把新功能打成AgentOS能加载的扩展包。同一个包装进WorkSwarm后就叫系统插件。
在「我的扩展」里启用后，就能回到手头的任务里试试。哪里用着不顺手，再告诉Agent怎么改。这就是openJiuwen所说的「Agent所想即所得」。
从WorkSwarm把自己变成桌宠说起，看看RSI原生AgentOS怎么让Agent给自己加功能
想随手跟Agent聊两句，或者临时交代件小事，桌面上有个能对话的桌宠就够了。碰到要来回查资料、分几步处理的任务，再打开工作台。
WorkSwarm默认没有桌宠形态，那能不能让Agent自己加一个？
把需求直接告诉Agent，比如「给WorkSwarm加个桌宠吧，我想在桌面上点一下就能跟你聊天。」
Agent可以按你的描述生成扩展包，再把它作为「应用形态」系统插件装到WorkSwarm里。WorkSwarm背后的RSI原生AgentOS负责加载扩展，让这个系统插件在工作台上生效。
启用系统插件后，点一下切换按钮，工作台就收起来了，桌面上只留下桌宠。
可以选小蜜蜂，也可以换成胶囊样式。想发消息就点开桌宠。聊到一半要用工作台，双击桌宠就能回去，刚才的对话还在。
拆解openJiuwen RSI原生AgentOS：扩展包怎样改变界面、网关、服务端与Agent行为？
上一节里，WorkSwarm启用系统插件后，就能把自己变成桌宠。这个新功能接在什么地方，又是怎么跑起来的？
我们先来看openJiuwen RSI原生AgentOS把界面、网关和Agent的执行，分成了哪些部分。
从用户发出请求到Agent执行任务，系统主要分三层。
Web客户端负责显示界面、接收用户操作；Gateway负责接入和转发请求；Agent层由AgentServer管理会话，由Harness组织任务执行和工具调用。
三层都留了扩展入口，既能在界面上加功能，也能调整请求怎么处理、任务怎么执行。
沿着这套架构看，扩展能力可以被分成五个环节。
Client可以增加按钮、面板和设置项，Gateway可以接入鉴权或调整请求路由，AgentServer可以处理会话、消息和服务端命令。
再往执行环节看，Swarm可以定制多个Agent的协作规则、跟踪任务进展，Agent可以调整提示词，接入工具、MCP服务或子Agent。
这些改动通过扩展包交付。包里的manifest.json会写明包标识、版本、依赖和代码入口。涉及界面时，还可以声明组件要显示在输入区、侧栏或设置页的哪个位置。
有了扩展包，运行环境还得知道该由谁加载、什么时候调用里面的代码。安装时，系统读取并检查清单，按包ID和版本保存扩展包。加载时，Gateway和AgentServer分别选取由自己运行的包，确定要加载的版本和顺序，再把扩展代码里的处理函数注册到各自的事件总线。
当用户点击界面按钮、网关收到请求，或Agent开始组装提示词时，相应的组件会发出事件。事件总线找到匹配的处理函数并调用它。处理函数可以参与当前流程，也可以通过Ops调用组件开放的能力。需要刷新界面时，扩展还可以把更新所需的数据发回Web客户端。
选扩展点时，可以先确定要在什么时机介入，再看对应的组件开放了哪些Operation能力（Ops）。
openJiuwen的RSI原生AgentOS开放了多类扩展事件。下面是各类事件常见的触发时机。
- 会话与消息：发送或接收跨会话消息时，以及上下文用量更新时。
- Agent执行：Agent开始组装系统提示词时。
- Swarm协作：生成团队协作规则时，以及团队运行状态发生变化后。
- 界面交互：扩展界面就绪时，或用户点击按钮、选择选项时。
- 网关与服务端：网关分发请求前，或服务端处理已接入的命令时。
处理函数能调用哪些Ops，要看它在哪个组件里运行。以下是几类常用能力。
- 读取会话数据，包括历史消息、对话轮次和上下文用量。
- 登记Agent可用的工具，供Agent执行任务时调用。
- 查询团队信息，通过只读接口查看成员、任务进展和依赖关系。
- 更新工作台界面，在扩展声明的位置显示面板或刷新内容。
- 通过网关发起HTTP请求，访问策略允许的地址。
- 访问资源和状态，在授权范围内读取文件，保存扩展自己的配置和运行状态。
扩展包的结构、事件和Ops的完整清单及用法，都可以在openJiuwen扩展开发文档里查到。
WorkSwarm系统插件实战：从创建、安装到故障回退
基于RSI原生AgentOS的扩展机制，WorkSwarm能接入Agent做出的系统插件。想加什么功能，直接把需求告诉Agent。
装好后，在「我的扩展」里启用，试过之后再按反馈调整。系统插件引起故障时，还可以从存档点恢复之前的配置，再继续调试。
和Agent对话，边做边调试你的第一个系统插件
第一次做系统插件，可以用开发Skill和Agent对话，边做边调试。
比如要做Token Weather，可以说「在输入框上方加条状态栏，显示当前会话的Token用量，用晴天、多云等天气提示占用程度。」Agent可以按需求编写代码、打包并安装到WorkSwarm。
启用Token Weather系统插件后就能试用。要是觉得状态栏占地方，可以接着说「做得紧凑一点，保留用量百分比。」Agent会按反馈修改系统插件并重新加载，让你再试一遍。
也可以手动编写系统插件的声明和代码，再打成ZIP。如果有依赖项，就在声明里写明依赖和版本要求，WorkSwarm加载时会检查。
系统插件怎么安装和启用？
通过开发Skill生成的系统插件会自动装进WorkSwarm。手动安装有三种方式。
- 放入安装目录。把解压后的系统插件文件放进安装目录，WorkSwarm重启时会加载。
- 从扩展页面安装。点击侧边栏的「扩展」，在「系统插件」里找到想要的功能并下载安装。
- 通过命令安装。在WorkSwarm的对话框里，用/extension install安装本地系统插件。
在「我的扩展→系统插件」里，可以查看已安装系统插件的状态，也可以启用或禁用系统插件。
安装完成并确认系统插件已启用后，就可以验证功能。以Token Weather为例，打开对话，先看输入框上方有没有状态栏，再发一条消息。等Agent回复完，看看状态栏里的用量有没有更新。
系统插件引起故障，怎么恢复原来的配置？
试用新系统插件时，能回退配置，才有余地继续试、继续改。
比如启用后某个页面打不开，可以选择故障前的存档点，恢复当时的系统插件配置。回退后，重新打开出问题的页面，确认能正常使用，再继续调试。
RSI原生AgentOS的扩展能做什么？从定制自己的Agent应用，到支持团队协作和企业接入
借助RSI原生AgentOS的扩展能力，可以按自己的习惯调整应用界面，也可以查看单个Agent的工作过程，调整它做事的方式。
当任务需要多个Agent一起完成时，团队怎么分工、怎么交接，也能按项目需要定制。应用接入企业环境时，还可以按部署要求调整访问管理和Agent的运行方式。
前端界面定制：让Agent定制工作台界面，有你的风格，用着更顺手
前端界面扩展可以改变Agent应用的外观和交互。Agent可以按你的喜好调整主题，也可以在页面预留的位置加按钮、状态栏或面板，把常看的信息和常用的操作放到顺手的地方。
在WorkSwarm里，想换个界面风格，可以跟Agent说「给工作台做几套带动画的主题，我想在设置里切换。」Agent根据描述生成主题背景扩展包。装进WorkSwarm并启用对应的系统插件后，在设置页选一个主题，工作台就会换上对应的动态背景。
Agent Harness调整：让Agent的工作过程看得见，做事方式也能按需调整
单Agent扩展可以接入会话管理、任务执行等环节。比如，它可以把会话状态和上下文用量呈现出来，让用户看清Agent的工作过程。
到了执行环节，扩展还可以按任务需要补充上下文、调整提示词里的工作规则，或为Agent登记新的工具。
在WorkSwarm里，想知道长对话的上下文都用在哪儿，可以让Agent生成一个用于上下文监控的系统插件。
启用后，面板显示输入Token数和窗口占用率，并估算系统提示词、技能、工具定义和消息各占多少。
你还可以对比每次模型请求的输入用量，查看工具调用的状态和耗时，回看近期轮次的用量摘要和会话消息。
Swarm协作增强：从定制协作规则到跟踪任务进展，看清谁在做、做到哪
多个Agent一起做任务时，可以通过扩展把项目自己的分工和交接约定写进协作规则。任务开始后，扩展还能接收状态变化的通知，跟踪谁在做哪项任务、已经做到哪一步。
比如，任务分给几个Agent后，想看看各自做到了哪，可以用扩展包开发Skill，让Agent按描述生成团队协作可视化扩展包。
装进WorkSwarm并启用对应的系统插件后，在集群模式下，就能在一个视图里看到团队成员、各自负责的任务和任务之间的依赖。要是某项任务还在等待，就可以顺着依赖查到哪项前置工作还没完成。
企业接入适配：让WorkSwarm适配企业环境，接入和运行都可按需调整
企业接入时，可以借助RSI原生AgentOS的扩展能力，按部署需要调整账号接入和Agent的运行环境。
分布式部署时，Gateway和AgentServer可以分开运行。企业可以按业务需要选择Gateway连接的AgentServer，并在两侧分别加载所需的扩展。
比如，在Gateway侧接入鉴权或调整请求路由，在AgentServer侧为会话补充项目上下文，或调整服务端命令的参数和执行结果处理方式。需要隔离执行时，还可以通过适配器接入第三方沙箱，让Agent在选定的环境里运行命令和代码。
在WorkSwarm中，Gateway登录系统插件可以给应用入口加上登录页，并在请求进入业务流程前校验凭证。启用后，未登录的用户会看到登录页，受保护的请求会被拦下。登录后，浏览器会带上凭证，校验通过的请求可以继续处理。
在WorkSwarm里，新建单Agent会话时，系统插件可以提供Claude Code（CC）、Codex和openJiuwen三种Harness选项。选好后，由所选的Harness执行这次会话的任务、调用工具，前端界面也会随之切换。
结语
Agent做着任务，也能动手改自己。它可以把想到的改法做成RSI原生AgentOS能加载的扩展包，装进WorkSwarm后作为系统插件启用。
回到任务里试一试，再按反馈调整界面和能力。试过好用的系统插件，下次做任务还能接着用。这就是openJiuwen所说的「Agent所想即所得」。
随着更多环节向扩展开放，个人的使用习惯、团队的协作规则和企业的运行要求，都可以成为Agent调整自己的依据。
刚装好时，它有一个默认的样子。往后会变成什么样，它可以在一件件实际工作里自己改出来。
欢迎来WorkSwarm试试，和Agent一起做个你想要的新功能，装上你的第一个系统插件，再到社区分享试用的效果！
